name: Covenant AI
title: RT by @covenant_ai: PULSE (also called Delta weight sync) has become one of the most important ideas in RL infrastructure this year. Our paper, posted on February 3, explained why it loses nothing. At RL learning rates, about 99% of each step's weight updates disappear in the BF16 cast, so the inference workers never see them. Since then, @huggingface has built Delta Weight Sync for TRL and vLLM on that argument. @FireworksAI_HQ cites PULSE, and its ARCv3 compressor now makes the updates even smaller. This week @humansand reported pausing inference for only about 220 milliseconds per update on Blackwell GPUs. PULSE has now been accepted at AXIOM, a @NeurIPSConf 2026 workshop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03839

name: Joseph Jacks
title: RT by @JosephJacks_: The future of software In the limit, of course, software won't mean anything anymore. Everything digital will be instantly created at will. But in the interim period we'll wander through an increasingly odd in-between age for software. This transition periodwill be defined by three new precepts. Everflux software - instead of stepping from release to release, months apart, software now evolves continuously. Software creation has broken the sound barrier of our own keystrokes, and every model release pushes it faster. There is no reason to wait weeks or months for the next release when a single company merges over 30,000 code changes a day. Cyber capabilities are also progressing at an increasing pace. Bug and vulnerability fixes need to ship quickly and continuously. And every piece of software sits in a lattice of dependencies, each one now shipping at a blistering pace. Software will have to move accordingly fast just to keep from breaking as everything around it shifts. Translucent sources – A new territory has opened between open source and closed source. Today Claude will happily pick apart any Electron app, and any binary shipped with debug symbols has become a reverse-engineering playground for LLMs. In other words, much so-called closed-source software is now open source in all but name, and keeping code closed makes less and less sense. Even the notion of IP and copyright is breaking in software: Apps don't even need to be accessed to be reproduced. I'm writing this text on a personal text editor I prompted Claude to vibe-code from a few videos of people demoing editor features they liked. A mere description of the interface is increasingly enough for an LLM to rebuild the internals, whether or not they resemble the original. Software IP seems to be dissolving like cotton candy in a raccoon's paws. Bespoke features - Now that all software is open source, nothing prevents us from modifying everything. And personalization is just one prompt and a couple million tokens away, so there is absolutely no reason anymore to wait for someone else to add this feature you want. Everyone becomes their own product manager. Want a search box, an API bridge, a custom button? It's a couple of minutes away, mostly executed in the background of your daily life. Soon we'll want to personalize everything. A major challenge appears when bespoke features crash into our first tenet: everflux software. How do you customize software without cutting yourself off from upstream? I could fork it for good to add my search box, but I'd lose all future benefit from the software creator, be it new security updates or other updates to the rest of the software. How do you personalize software that was never meant to be personalized, without shouldering all of its future maintenance? Merge conflicts won't be the exception anymore; they'll be a constant of everflux software. Agents will rebase our personal features onto each new release overnight, and software will look less like a product and more like a living species, evolving through constant mutation. Image: M.C. Escher, Metamorphosis II, November 1939 - March 1940

name: Joseph Jacks
title: RT by @JosephJacks_: @planepowers real-time engine is coming. It's been almost three years since we started building Plane, and the response has been overwhelming from day one. First our open-source Community Edition, then our first cloud plan, then the commercial self-hosted edition, and then air-gapped. Yes, it's a lot. We serve Plane in four very different environments, and we're not a single product anymore either. Many customers move to Plane because of fragmentation. They use one tool to manage projects, one for knowledge and one for support. Real-time became our top priority within a year of starting Plane. But at the pace we move, it kept slipping, and our community kept asking for it on GitHub and our forum. Surprisingly, around the same time, some of the enterprises we work with weren't ready for a product that worked in real time at all. That was a little sad, but let me explain. One customer moving away from Jira had a Save button on the work item description. Nothing was saved until someone clicked it. They didn't want to experiment with conflict-free editing, and wanted to keep their manual saves and their own version control. Pages in Plane have been collaborative for a while, and teams coming from Confluence asked us to turn that off and give them a Save button too. That taught us something. People trust what they can see saved, so real-time has to be at least as trustworthy as that button. Our first approach was a local database. In late 2024 we shipped Hyper Mode, which kept your work items in SQLite inside the browser, so switching layouts and filters felt instant. But it needed HTTPS, so self-hosted teams on local networks fell back to the API, and big projects slowed it down. A fast local copy is still a copy, too. Your teammate's change didn't reach you any sooner, and we retired it in 2025. The second was WebSockets. Open a socket, tell every tab that something changed, and let it refetch. That works in a demo. With a real team, two people move the same card at once, and laptops wake up with stale tabs. And every update must reach only the people allowed to see it. Plane confidently showing you the wrong thing is worse than making you refresh. So we started from the database. Every change in Plane is written to Postgres, and in the same transaction a trigger records it as an event. Our real-time engine reads that stream, checks who is allowed to see each change, and sends it in order to every open tab. If a tab drops off, it catches up as soon as it's back. It runs on the Postgres, RabbitMQ and Redis that Plane already ships with. Nothing in it depends on a third-party service, which matters when the customer is air-gapped. We've grown so much, and honestly, real-time was the one thing we couldn't rush. We took the time to get it right without breaking anything for the teams already on Plane. Plane is going real-time. Soon.

name: Oro
title: R to @oroagents: For AI to be a productive economic actor, it will have to learn the tacit knowledge that lives with the people who do these jobs, and learn it the same way we do, from the results of its decisions. SMB Bench is a high-fidelity simulation grounded in real, public data in which that learning can be observed. With it, we have taken a step in identifying the gaps in AI running a profitable autonomous business. We think this is one of the most important problems in AI right now, and we are only getting started. If it excites you too, please reach out, we would love to talk: team@oroagents.com

name: Opentensor Foundation
title: RT by @opentensor: The economic value of agents will soon come from running whole autonomous businesses, not just from finishing one-off tasks. When you run a business, the result of your own decisions arrive weeks later. You have to notice them, trace them to something you did, and act before they compound. Today, we're excited to announce SMB Bench, where we measure all the frontier models' ability to observe changes in the environment and adapt accordingly.
